children: India’s global manufacturing opportunity is moving beyond its traditional cost advantage as companies increasingly compete on complex supply chains, specialised capabilities and the ability to meet demanding international standards across sectors ranging from electrical equipment to nuclear energy.

Industry leaders at the IEEMA Annual Convention 2026 in Mumbai said the next stage of international expansion will require Indian manufacturers to identify specific customer problems, build capabilities around them and become deeply integrated into global supply chains rather than approaching exports primarily through geography or lower production costs.

Bharat Jaisinghani, Joint Managing Director, Polycab India Ltd., said Indian manufacturing has historically been viewed internationally through the lens of cost competitiveness. “They said, ‘We define you as India’s low-cost country’,” Jaisinghani said.

Polycab’s experience suggests that the more durable advantage comes from solving manufacturing and supply-chain problems that are expensive or difficult for customers to manage elsewhere. The company can simultaneously supply roughly 6,000 to 7,000 SKUs, creating significant engineering and operational complexity. “If one can consistently solve a specific problem, a brand gets developed,” Jaisinghani said.
Customer Problems Over Geography

That approach is also changing how companies identify international markets. Rather than choosing a geography and then seeking opportunities within it, manufacturers can identify customer categories whose requirements remain broadly similar across countries. “More than geography, it is defining the type of the customer,” Jaisinghani said.

Data centres are one such segment today, while oil and gas represented a major global opportunity during an earlier investment cycle. Understanding the problems faced by a particular category of customers can therefore provide a more scalable route into multiple international markets. “Those customers are the same all over the world, or their challenges are similar all over,” Jaisinghani said.

KEC International’s manufacturing approach similarly takes into account production economics, customer requirements and response times while determining whether equipment should be supplied from India or from its manufacturing operations elsewhere. The model allows the company to use India as part of a broader international manufacturing network rather than treating exports as a standalone activity.

For Indian companies, the implication is that global competitiveness will increasingly depend on matching the right manufacturing location with the right customer requirement. Cost remains important, but responsiveness, engineering capability, product complexity and the ability to manage multiple markets are becoming equally significant differentiators.

The opportunity is particularly visible in sectors where global buyers are actively seeking additional manufacturing capacity. EDF, one of Europe’s largest nuclear operators and developers, is already engaging Indian companies for its international supply chain even though it does not currently have an operational nuclear project in India. “This is for our purchase in India today,” said Owen Xavier, Supply Chain Development & Localisation Lead, EDF – Développement Nucléaire International, France.

EDF has worked with more than 200 suppliers in India and maintains a database of over 1,000 companies as it assesses capabilities that could support its international nuclear programme. “What we can do is work with your companies, help them into our global supply chain,” Xavier said.
Moving Into Higher Value Manufacturing

Entering nuclear supply chains, however, illustrates the capability jump required for Indian manufacturers seeking higher-value international business. EDF expects suppliers to demonstrate nuclear-grade quality systems alongside extensive documentation and traceability covering the journey from raw materials through manufacturing, delivery, installation and commissioning. “We need full traceability,” Xavier said.

Manufacturers must also demonstrate oversight of their own vendors and processes to prevent counterfeit, fraudulent and suspect items from entering the supply chain. In nuclear projects, failures in this area can have consequences extending beyond an individual supplier to the vendor and the project itself. “You need to demonstrate a full oversight of your supply chain,” Xavier said.

The volumes involved can be substantial even while quality requirements remain stringent. Xavier cited nearly 2,000 kilometres of cables being required for a single nuclear unit, creating an opportunity for manufacturers capable of combining scale with consistent compliance. “We need Indian suppliers to be able to match our requirements,” he said.

EDF sees the transition into nuclear manufacturing as a staged process rather than expecting suppliers to immediately manufacture the most critical components. Indian companies can begin with conventional island and balance-of-plant packages before building towards more specialised and higher-value requirements. “You need to start the journey slowly,” Xavier said.

The company is also conducting pre-qualification assessments to identify gaps before suppliers enter formal qualification. Its process includes factory-floor assessments and a 60-question framework spanning eight areas, followed by feedback intended to help companies improve their readiness. “We work hand in hand,” Xavier said.

Such investments require a longer-term approach than conventional export orders. Nuclear projects can involve years of development and construction followed by decades of operation and eventual decommissioning, requiring suppliers capable of sustaining relationships and technical support over extended periods. “A nuclear project has a 100-year cycle,” Xavier said.

For Indian manufacturers, the emerging global opportunity is therefore not simply about producing the same equipment more cheaply. Building international scale will increasingly require companies to solve difficult customer problems, invest in specialised capabilities and demonstrate that they can deliver consistently against global technical and quality requirements.

The shift could move Indian manufacturing from being primarily perceived as a cost-efficient sourcing destination towards becoming a strategic part of global industrial supply chains. As Xavier put it, international projects require “genuine local capability and long-term value creation.”
